323.title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137)
323.hook: exiles hang up their harps and ask how to sing in a strange land
323.howItsDone: Many Jews say Psalm 137 before Grace after Meals on weekdays, and at many weddings 'If I forget thee, O Jerusalem' is recited or sung just before the groom breaks a glass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mizmor, the Sabbath song: the righteous flourish like a palm, still bearing fruit in old age. Now, a much sadder song.

A song from back home comes on in a supermarket. A neighbor cooks a dish a grandmother used to make. Homesickness can arrive that small: three notes, one smell, and the place you live is suddenly somewhere else. Psalm one thirty-seven comes from a far bigger loss. Home was a burned city, and the road out of it ended in a foreign empire. Someone among those exiles made a song about it. It's still sung, and its oath is still said at many Jewish weddings.
screen: `A SONG FROM BACK HOME.` → `THREE NOTES, ONE SMELL.` → `MARCHED AWAY TO BABYLON.`

segments.voice: The Book of Kings tells it plainly: the Babylonian army burned the Temple and the city, and carried many of the people off into exile. Psalm one thirty-seven sings from that exile. "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." On the willows there, they hung up their harps. Their captors, the psalm says, asked for entertainment: sing us one of the songs of Zion. They answer with a question. How can we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land? It's an exile's question: can you keep your faith, your music, your self, far from the place it belongs? Then comes the oath: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I don't remember you, if I don't set Jerusalem above my highest joy. That oath became part of Jewish life. At many weddings, just before the groom breaks the glass, someone says it. At the happiest moment, a memory of loss. The psalm doesn't end gently. Its last lines are a cry of fury at the people who destroyed their city, so raw it's hard to read. It doesn't hide that grief can turn into rage. Some readers say that is the point: the rage is put into words and brought before God, not acted out. And the harps? The psalm leaves them hanging on the willows. But the song itself was carried, and it is still sung far from Jerusalem.
screen: `JERUSALEM FALLS TO BABYLON.` · `HARPS ON THE WILLOWS.` · `HOW CAN WE SING HERE?` · `THE OATH AT THE WEDDING.` · then, large: `IF I FORGET THEE.`

segments.voice: Think of a place you miss, or a time, or a person: a childhood home, a city, a grandmother's kitchen, a version of yourself. Let the missing come up, without pushing it away or drowning in it, and sit beside it the way the exiles sat by the river; then ask what from that place you can still carry here, a song, a habit, a way of being. If you pray, bring your longing to God.
Zion. The Jerusalem the exiles of Psalm one thirty-seven wept for, hung up their harps for, and swore never to forget.
Your line: if I forget thee. Even at the happiest moment, there's room to remember. See you tomorrow.

324.title: Out of the depths (Psalm 130)
324.hook: a cry from the deep, said in the days before Yom Kippur
324.carry: more than watchmen for the morning
324.howItsDone: In many communities, Psalm 130 is said aloud in the morning service during the Ten Days of Repentance between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and many people recite it in times of trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zion: exiles by the rivers of Babylon, swearing, if I forget thee. Today, another cry from a low place.

Three in the morning, awake, staring at the ceiling. Something has gone badly wrong, or you've done something you regret, and it feels like you're at the bottom of a well, too far down for anyone to hear. Everything polite has fallen away. What comes out, if anything comes out, isn't a speech. It's a cry. There's a psalm for exactly that place, and it's only eight verses long.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `THE BOTTOM OF A WELL.` → `NOT A SPEECH. A CRY.`

segments.voice: Psalm one thirty is one of fifteen psalms with the heading Song of Ascents. The Mishnah describes fifteen steps in the Temple where the Levites stood and sang, and many connect these songs to those steps, or to pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem. This one climbs from the very bottom. "Out of the depths" have I called You, O Lord. In Hebrew, mi-ma'amakim: the depths of the sea, the pit, the lowest place. Hasidic teachers love a second reading: not only from my deep trouble, but from deep inside me, the bottom of the heart, where nothing is fake. Then an honest admission. If You kept a record of every wrong, Lord, who could stand? But with You there is forgiveness. The psalm doesn't pretend to be innocent. It asks for mercy. Then its most beautiful image: my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning. Picture a guard on the night shift, staring east for the first gray light that tells him the night is over. The psalm says the line twice, as if the night is that long. That's why, in many communities, this psalm is said every morning in the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: days for honest accounting, said from the depths, waiting for the light.
screen: `A SONG OF ASCENTS.` · `MI-MA'AMAKIM: FROM THE DEPTHS.` · `WHO COULD STAND?` · `WATCHMEN WAITING FOR MORNING.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS.`

segments.voice: Go down, gently, to the lowest place in you right now: something you're sorry for, something you're afraid of, something you need. Don't dress it up; find the fewest words that say it, maybe just help, or I'm sorry, or I'm scared, and say it inside, once, from the bottom. Then wait, the way a watchman waits for the morning, and if you pray, say it to God.
Mi-ma'amakim. From the depths, or from deep inside — Psalm one thirty's cry said in the days before Yom Kippur: my soul waits, more than watchmen for the morning.
Your line: more than watchmen for the morning. A cry from the depths, and then the waiting. Day three hundred twenty-four, done.

325.title: Unto the mountains (Psalm 121)
325.hook: "He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep"
325.howItsDone: Many Jews recite Psalm 121 before travel, at a sickbed and for protection in childbirth; it is often printed on cards or plaques placed near a newborn, and it is part of the Shabbat afternoon psalms in some communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mi-ma'amakim: a cry from the depths, waiting more than watchmen for the morning. Today, eyes up.

In some Jewish homes, a small printed card hangs near a newborn's crib. Others keep the same words folded in a wallet for a long drive, or tucked into a suitcase. Eight short verses, turning on one plain fact about people: sooner or later, guards doze and parents nod off. Nobody can keep watch forever. The psalm on the card says there is a keeper who can. It starts with a traveler looking up at the hills.
screen: `A CARD BY THE CRIB.` → `GUARDS DOZE, PARENTS NOD OFF.` → `A KEEPER WHO DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: It's another Song of Ascents, often read as a pilgrim's song. A traveler on the road to Jerusalem looks up at the hills ahead. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: from whence shall my help come?" Some readers hear worry in the question: hills are where danger can hide on a long road. The answer comes straight back: my help comes from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth. Not from the mountains; from the One who made them. Then the great promise: "Behold, He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep." The Hebrew word is shomer: a keeper, a guard, someone who stays alert while others rest. In just eight verses, forms of that word appear six times. The Lord is your keeper. He'll keep you from all evil, keep your going out and your coming in, from now and forever. The sun won't strike you by day, nor the moon by night. That's why many Jews say this psalm for protection: before a journey, for a woman giving birth, at a sickbed. Hasidic teachers found a hidden reading in the opening question. From where, me-ayin, can also be heard as from ayin, from nothingness. In that reading, help begins the moment a person admits there is nothing left. And under it stands the psalm's promise: a keeper who stays awake when you can't.

segments.voice: Look at a hill, a skyline or the edge of the sky, or close your eyes and picture mountains far off, and notice how different it feels to look up and out instead of down. Ask the psalm's question quietly, where will my help come from, and picture the people you watch over kept, even while you sleep. If you pray, say the psalm's promise.
Shomer. A keeper, a guard, one who stays alert while others rest — the word Psalm one twenty-one uses six times for the One who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
Your line: he doesn't sleep. Someone else can hold the night shift. That's day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: Psalm 27 in Elul
326.hook: said through the month before the High Holy Days: wait for the Lord, be strong
326.howItsDone: From the start of Elul through the High Holy Day season, many communities add Psalm 27 to morning and afternoon or evening prayers, and Ashkenazi communities blow the shofar each weekday morning of Elul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shomer: the keeper of Israel, who neither slumbers nor sleeps. Today, a month of getting ready.

Athletes have a preseason. Actors have rehearsals. Before a wedding there are weeks of fittings and planning and nerves. Nobody walks into the big day cold. The Jewish year works the same way. Before the High Holy Days, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, comes a whole month of warming up. In many communities it has its own sound, the shofar blown on weekday mornings, and its own psalm, said every day, often twice. That month is Elul.
screen: `A PRESEASON, A REHEARSAL.` → `NOBODY WALKS IN COLD.` → `A MONTH TO WARM UP.`

segments.voice: Elul is the last month of the Jewish year, right before Rosh Hashanah: a month for turning around, teshuvah, getting ready to stand before God. Tradition hears a hint in its four letters, aleph, lamed, vav, lamed. They're the first letters of a line from the Song of Songs: ani le-dodi ve-dodi li, I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine. So Elul isn't only a time of fear. It's a time of closeness. Every day of Elul, many communities add Psalm twenty-seven. It opens with courage: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" An old midrash reads it as a map of the season ahead. My light: Rosh Hashanah. My salvation: Yom Kippur. Later teachers added a third: when the psalm says God will hide me in His shelter, the Hebrew word comes from sukkah, so they heard Sukkot, the festival that comes after. Read that way, the psalm walks through the whole holiday season. But it's honest, too. The middle gets shaky: hide not Your face from me; even if my father and mother leave me. It isn't the voice of someone who has it all together. Then the last line, the one Elul hangs on: "Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let thy heart take courage; yea, wait thou for the LORD." Wait, be strong, wait again. Getting ready isn't about having answers. It's about staying, with courage, until the day comes.
screen: `ELUL: THE MONTH BEFORE.` · `I AM MY BELOVED'S.` · `LIGHT, SALVATION, SHELTER.` · `WAIT, BE STRONG, WAIT.` · then, large: `WAIT, AND BE STRONG.`

segments.voice: If you can, find Psalm twenty-seven and read all fourteen verses slowly, noticing where it's brave and where it trembles. If not, sit with its first line, the Lord is my light, whom shall I fear, and let one fear come up; then with its last, wait, and be strong, staying beside that fear with a little courage, without solving it today. If you pray, say the psalm as your prayer.
Elul. The month before the High Holy Days: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine. Its psalm ends: wait for the Lord, be strong.
Your line: wait, and be strong. Elul is for closeness, not only fear. Until tomorrow.

327.title: Sow in tears (Psalm 126)
327.hook: sung before grace on Shabbat: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy"
327.carry: sow in tears, reap in joy
327.howItsDone: On Shabbat and festivals, many families sing Psalm 126, Shir ha-ma'alot, before Grace after Meals, often to lively tunes that everyone at the table knows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elul, the month before the High Holy Days, and its psalm: wait, and be strong.

Thump, thump, thump. Hands on the tablecloth, keeping time. It's Shabbat or a festival, the long meal is over, plates pushed back, a few crumbs of challah left, kids getting restless. Before the grace after meals, someone starts a song and the whole table joins in, often loudly. Shir ha-ma'alot: a Song of Ascents. In many families it's the sound of a full, happy table. And right in the middle of it are the words: sow in tears.
screen: `HANDS DRUMMING THE TABLE.` → `THE WHOLE TABLE SINGS.` → `AND IN THE MIDDLE: TEARS.`

segments.voice: Psalm one twenty-six remembers a homecoming. When the Lord brought the exiles back to Zion, it says, we were like people dreaming. Our mouths filled with laughter, our tongues with song. Even the nations said: God has done great things for them. Some readers hear it as the other side of Psalm one thirty-seven: the ones who wept by the rivers of Babylon come home, and it feels too good to be real. In many Ashkenazi homes the two even share the table: one thirty-seven before grace on weekdays, one twenty-six on Shabbat. Then a prayer: bring back the rest of us, like streams in the Negev, the southern desert, where dry riverbeds suddenly flood after rain. And then the farming picture: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." A farmer walks out weeping, carrying a bag of seed, and comes home with joy, carrying sheaves. Why weep while sowing? One common reading: in a hard year, seed is food a family chooses not to eat. It goes into the ground on a hope, with grief and trust at the same time. The dreaming line has a story attached. The Talmud says it puzzled Honi, the circle-drawer from weeks ago: how could seventy years of exile pass like a dream? His answer began with a man planting a carob tree for his descendants, a tree whose fruit the planter would never eat. That's sowing in tears. So at a full Shabbat table, the song is about tears, because the joy at the table grew from seeds someone once sowed, crying.
screen: `LIKE PEOPLE DREAMING.` · `STREAMS IN THE NEGEV.` · `SEED YOU CHOOSE NOT TO EAT.` · `HONI AND THE CAROB TREE.` · then, large: `SOW IN TEARS, REAP IN JOY.`

segments.voice: Think of something hard you're doing whose fruit you can't see yet: raising a child, healing, learning, saving, rebuilding something broken. Picture it as a seed in the ground and say, inside, what you hope it grows into; if you have a seed, a cutting or a bulb at hand, you can plant it with that hope. If you pray, ask for the harvest.
Shir ha-ma'alot. A Song of Ascents, sung before grace on Shabbat: the exiles came home like dreamers, and they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Your line: sow in tears, reap in joy. Tears going out, sheaves coming home. Day three hundred twenty-seven, in the books.

328.title: Psalms for the sick
328.hook: communities divide the whole book to read for someone who is ill
328.howItsDone: Jewish communities organize Tehillim groups that divide the Book of Psalms for someone who is ill, name them in the Mi she-berakh prayer at the Torah reading, and wish them refuah shlemah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shir ha-ma'alot, the song before grace: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.

The news comes into the group chat late at night. Someone's mother is in the hospital. It's serious. Within an hour, something happens that's become common in Jewish communities: a list appears. Psalms one to ten, Sarah. Eleven to twenty, David. Twenty-one to thirty, the Cohens. By the next evening, a whole community of people, some of whom have never met the sick woman, has read the entire Book of Psalms for her.
screen: `A MESSAGE LATE AT NIGHT.` → `A LIST APPEARS.` → `THE WHOLE BOOK, FOR ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Saying psalms for someone who is ill is a custom kept in many Jewish communities. When there's nothing else to do, this is something to do. Often it's shared: a group divides all one hundred fifty psalms, so the whole book gets said for one person, sometimes every day. The person is named the Hebrew way, with their own name and their mother's: Sarah, daughter of Rachel. Some add a custom with Psalm one nineteen, the long psalm arranged by the Hebrew alphabet: they read the sections whose letters spell the sick person's name. Some psalms are often chosen. Psalm twenty: "The LORD answer thee in the day of trouble". Psalm thirty, the song of someone who cried out and was healed. And the prayer for healing goes back to the Torah. When Moses' sister Miriam became ill, Moses cried out five short Hebrew words: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." No long speech. Just her, and now. Jews also say a prayer called Mi she-berakh for the sick when the Torah is read, and wish each other refuah shlemah, a complete healing, of body and spirit. The psalms don't replace doctors; Jewish tradition values medicine deeply. The Talmud teaches that visiting the sick is itself a kind of healing. But when you're far away, or the waiting room has gone quiet, or there's nothing left to try, a psalm is something you can hold, together.

segments.voice: Think of someone who is sick right now, in body or in spirit, picture their face, and say their name quietly. If you can, find Psalm twenty or Psalm thirty and read it for them; if not, use Moses' five words, heal her now, or heal him now, or just hold them in your mind with a wish for a complete healing. If you pray, pray for them in your own words.
Refuah shlemah. A complete healing, of body and spirit — the wish said for someone who is ill, as communities divide the whole Book of Psalms to read for them.
Your line: something you can hold, together. A whole book, shared out, for one person. That's three hundred twenty-eight.

329.title: Everything that breathes (Psalm 150)
329.hook: the book ends: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD"
329.carry: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord
329.howItsDone: Psalm 150 is said every morning as the last of the psalms of praise (Pesukei de-Zimra), and many repeat its final verse to mark the end of the Book of Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, refuah shlemah: a complete healing, and a community reading the whole book for one person. Today, the last psalm of all.

A great concert doesn't end quietly. The band brings everything in at once: drums, horns, guitars, the crowd singing along, the lights all on. On the last song, nobody holds anything back. The Book of Psalms ends the same way. After a hundred and forty-nine songs of joy and grief, fear and hope, exile and homecoming, the very last psalm is pure, loud, everything-at-once praise. And its final line is about something you're doing right now. Breathing.
screen: `THE LAST SONG OF THE CONCERT.` → `EVERYTHING AT ONCE.` → `THE LAST LINE: BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Psalm one fifty is short, only six verses, and almost every line starts the same way: hallelu, praise. Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him for His mighty acts. Then the instruments pour in: the blast of the shofar, harp and lyre, drum and dance, strings and pipe, loud cymbals, crashing cymbals. It's the whole orchestra of ancient Israel, all at once. Then the last line of the whole book: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Hallelujah. After all the instruments, the final one is breath. Not only priests or Levites or musicians: every person, every animal, anyone who can draw air. Jews say this psalm every morning, near the end of the psalms of praise that open the service, and many repeat that last line twice, to mark the end. The rabbis noticed that the word for breath, neshamah, is also the word for soul. A midrash plays on it: read neshamah as neshimah, a single breath, and it says, for every single breath you take, praise God. Not once a day. Every breath. So the Book of Psalms, and these two weeks of psalms, end with breath. They began with a tree by the water, then the stars, the shepherd, the mountain, the open hand, a song for each day, Hallel, and Shabbat. This week: the rivers of Babylon, the depths, the mountains, Elul, sowing in tears, refuah shlemah, and now, everything that breathes.
screen: `HALLELU: PRAISE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SHOFAR, HARP, DRUM, CYMBALS.` · `THE LAST INSTRUMENT IS BREATH.` · `NESHAMAH: BREATH AND SOUL.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if you like, and take one slow breath in and one slow breath out: that breath is the last instrument of the Book of Psalms.
